# Was the Expedia data breach a hack?

**Confirmed.** A vendor-side attack, yes: Expedia confirmed, per Skift, that attackers got in through a compromised third-party data platform provider. What was taken is not established.

Incident: Expedia third-party vendor breach, Nov 2026. Also reported as the Expedia supply chain attack and the Expedia data leak. First published Nov 22, 2026; last updated Nov 22, 2026, 3:31 PM ET.

Picture: The south entrance of Expedia Group's headquarters in Seattle. Image: T014y, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Expedia_Group_south_entrance.jpg).

> **Not verified: initial investigation only.** Nothing on this page is absolutely confirmed. It is an early look based only on publicly available sources, and it should not be treated as verified fact. Even items labeled "Confirmed" only mean a public source reports them. Made for entertainment using AI. Not endorsed by Expedia, Skift, Cybernews, The Seattle Times or any other company, news outlet, government agency, or anyone else named.

This is the current answer, not a final verdict.

## The latest

Nov 22, 2026, 3:31 PM ET: **A second outlet describes the group's posted Expedia files: hundreds of thousands of emails, possibly old; still not confirmed by Expedia.** New source: Cyber Daily (s008, Tier 2, Nov 12 Australian time), independent of Cybernews. It dates the group's leak post to Nov 3 (new timeline row t005), quotes the same claimed figures and says the posted extract lists hundreds of thousands of email addresses linked to travel data, some seen in earlier breaches, possibly historical. Added to c003, c004 (still Unverified: two outlets relay the group's claim but nobody has checked it) and c005 (still Reported: the files are not confirmed as Expedia's). No label change on any claim or the main question. Checked: no Expedia newsroom post or customer notice; no Form 8-K with Item 1.05 on EDGAR (latest 8-K Nov 4, earnings); no Qubole or Idera statement; no new Expedia statement since Nov 18. Staleness check done: head, known, not known, figures and size still accurate. Privacy check done: no staff, researchers, reporters, plaintiffs or contacts named. The group's page was not visited.

## At a glance

- Status: monitoring
- Size: Regional. Unconfirmed. A group claims about a billion records; roughly 500MB has been posted, per Cybernews. Expedia has not said what was exposed.
- Who is affected: Not yet clear. A posted dataset is said to hold traveler emails, bookings and loyalty details. Expedia has not confirmed that. Watch for fake booking emails.

| Value | What | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| 1B | Records claimed | Unverified; by n0n, per Cybernews |
| 500MB+ | Posted so far | Per Cybernews |

### Known so far

- Expedia confirmed attackers got in through a compromised third-party data platform provider.

### Not known yet

- Whether the billion-record claim is true.
- Whether customer data was taken, and whose.
- Which vendor, and how the attacker got in.

## What we checked and did not find

We looked for these and did not find them as of 3:31 PM ET on Nov 22, 2026.

- An Expedia newsroom page or customer notice. The statement appears only as quotes to Skift and The Seattle Times.
- The name of the vendor, or how the attacker got in.
- Expedia saying whether customer data was taken, or confirming the posted files are real.
- Any independent check of the group's claimed volume. Cyber Daily reports the group claimed more than one terabyte, and Cybernews says it claimed a billion records.
- Any regulator filing or customer notice. Expedia's SEC filings show no Form 8-K under Item 1.05, the item for a material cyber incident; its latest 8-K, on Nov 4, is about earnings.
- Any public statement from Qubole or its parent company, Idera.
- Any link, confirmed by Expedia or researchers, between this breach and the Qubole attack.

Part of the Skift article is behind a subscription; we read the start of Expedia's quote and Skift's summary. We did not visit the group's leak page.
